purpose: Measure whether a handset hears an Egyptian Cook correctly, before any model sees the words. Read docs/ops/measuring-transcription.md before using this.

scoring.exact: The transcript matches one of `accept` exactly. Best case.
scoring.equivalent: Different spelling, same word, and a model would read it the same. Counts as a pass — Arabic orthography varies and the downstream model tolerates it.
scoring.msa_substituted: The recogniser returned the Modern Standard equivalent in `msa_trap` instead of what was said. THIS IS THE METRIC THAT DECIDES T083. It means the engine is transcribing Egyptian speech through a non-Egyptian model, and every Cook in Egypt hits it.
scoring.wrong: Something else, or nothing. Note whether it was silence, a truncation, or a different word.

how_to_read_the_result: An msa_substituted rate above roughly 20% on the `msa_lexical` set means on-device recognition is not serving Egyptian Arabic, whatever the raw accuracy looks like. Loanword and dish failures matter more than sentence failures: a Cook can rephrase a sentence, but if the phone cannot hear بانيه there is no rephrasing that helps, and no downstream model recovers a dish name it never received.

utterances.why: The single most common protein a Cook will say. Egyptian uses فراخ; every MSA-trained model reaches for دجاج.
One letter apart in writing, clearly different when spoken. A cheap probe for which dialect model is loaded.
عيش means bread in Egypt and life in MSA. A substitution here changes meaning, not just spelling.
Deep colloquial Cairene for tomato. A recogniser that returns طماطم is still usable; one that returns nothing is not.
The verb a Cook actually uses to start. If this comes back as MSA the whole conversation register is wrong.
No MSA speaker says this. Pure dialect marker.
Negation is structural. Getting it wrong can invert an allergen or spice statement.
Named explicitly in .claude/rules/ai.md as a case the product must handle.
The word T083 was written around. Extremely common on Egyptian menus and absent from most dictionaries.
Loanword that collides with real Arabic roots, so a weak model has something wrong to reach for.
Brand name turned common noun. Purely Egyptian usage.
Loanword with unstable spelling — tests whether `equivalent` scoring is doing real work.
Cairene pronounces ج as a hard g. A model trained on Levantine or Gulf audio expects a j and may miss the word entirely.
Cairene realises ق as a glottal stop — 'ahwa, not qahwa. The clearest single test of whether the acoustic model is Egyptian.
Same hard-g test on a food word, so a failure is attributable to phonology rather than vocabulary.
Hard g plus emphatic consonants in one short phrase, which is how these actually arrive.
Egypt's national dish. If this fails, nothing else about the feature matters.
Common, and phonetically long enough that a partial match is informative.
Two-word dish name. Tests whether the second word survives when the first is recognised.
Distinctly Egyptian, unlikely to appear in a general Arabic lexicon.
A dish name made of two ordinary words, so a recogniser may transcribe it correctly yet a naive matcher would still need to treat it as one dish.
The hardest dish name in common use. Expect this one to fail even on a good engine.

utterances.say: عملت كشري بالعدس والحمص، الوصفة بتاعة ماما
accept: عملت كشري بالعدس والحمص الوصفة بتاعة ماما
utterances.why: A whole first answer, exactly as a Cook would give it. Score per word, not whole-string.

utterances.say: ملوخية خضرا بالفراخ والرز، وكمان شوية شطة
accept: ملوخية خضرا بالفراخ والرز وكمان شوية شطة
utterances.why: Carries the فراخ trap inside a natural sentence, where surrounding context might rescue it — or might not.
Allergen words spoken aloud. A mistranscription here is the highest-consequence failure in the product, because a Customer reads the result as fact.
Spoken numbers, which recognisers render inconsistently as words or digits. Price is money, so the parser must handle both — and this records which one arrives.
